title: Asking for sources, 2026
source: Captured by Paul Kwiatkowski on 2026-09-16 with the same five prompts used in the 2023 manual. Replies reproduced as recorded, including formatting. Images are shown as placeholders.

messages.text: I'm in grade 10 and need to do some research for a report about Hadrian's Wall. Can you suggest some sources?

Absolutely. For a Grade 10 report, I’d recommend using **a mix of reliable historical websites, archaeological evidence, and at least one book or academic source** rather than relying on Wikipedia alone.

### Good starting sources

1. **[English Heritage – History of Hadrian’s Wall](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/history/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)**
   Probably the best place to start. It covers **why the Wall was built, when it was constructed, its length, Roman Britain, forts, and how the Wall changed over time**. English Heritage is responsible for many of the archaeological sites along the Wall. ([English Heritage][1])

2. **[UNESCO – Frontiers of the Roman Empire](https://www.unesco.org/en/world-heritage/frontiers-roman-empire?utm_source=chatgpt.com)**
   Useful if your report discusses **why Hadrian's Wall was historically important** or why it is a World Heritage Site. UNESCO explains the Wall as part of the much larger frontier system of the Roman Empire. ([UNESCO][2])

3. **[Historic England – Hadrian’s Wall](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000098?utm_source=chatgpt.com)**
   A good source for **archaeological and historical significance**. It is especially useful if you need evidence about the Wall as a military frontier rather than just a tourist attraction. ([Historic England][3])

4. **[English Heritage – Research on Hadrian’s Wall](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/history/research/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)**
   This is a little more advanced, but excellent for a Grade 10 report. It discusses **archaeological excavations, Vindolanda writing tablets, geophysical surveys, dating techniques, and unanswered questions**. It also points out that less than 5% of the Wall has been archaeologically examined, which is interesting if you want to discuss limitations of historical evidence. ([English Heritage][4])

5. **[English Heritage – Sources for Hadrian’s Wall](https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/history/sources/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)**
   If you need **more academic sources**, use this bibliography. It lists books, archaeological reports, inscriptions, writing tablets, museums, and scholarly articles about the Wall. ([English Heritage][5])

### One particularly interesting source of evidence

Look into the **Vindolanda writing tablets**. These are actual Roman documents discovered near Hadrian's Wall and include letters and other records written by people living around the frontier. They can give you evidence about **ordinary soldiers and civilians**, rather than just emperors and battles. English Heritage identifies the tablets as one of the major developments in our understanding of life on the Roman frontier. ([English Heritage][4])

### A possible Grade 10 research structure

If you're not sure what to investigate, you could organize your report around:

* **What was Hadrian's Wall?**
* **Why did Emperor Hadrian order it to be built?**
* **How was it constructed?**
* **Who built and defended it?**
* **What was daily life like along the Wall?**
* **Did it actually keep people out, or did it serve other purposes?**
* **What happened to the Wall after the Romans left Britain?**
* **What can archaeologists learn from the remaining evidence?**
* **Why is Hadrian's Wall important today?**

That last-but-one question could make your report particularly interesting because historians **don't know everything about the Wall**; archaeological evidence has actually changed some interpretations of how it worked and what its purpose was. ([English Heritage][4])

If this is for an **IB/MYP Grade 10 report**, I can also give you **5–8 sources specifically chosen for reliability and usefulness, with a short explanation of what evidence you could take from each one and how to cite them**.

Did Emperor Hadrian ever visit the wall?

Yes — **Emperor Hadrian did visit Britain in AD 122**, and his visit is closely connected with the decision to build Hadrian’s Wall. ([English Heritage][1])

However, there's an important distinction:

* **Hadrian definitely visited Britain in AD 122.**
* During that visit, he inspected the army and the northern frontier.
* The Wall was begun around AD 122, following his visit.
* **There is no strong evidence that Hadrian personally walked along the completed Wall.** In fact, the Wall took several years to construct, and Hadrian left Britain after his relatively brief visit and continued travelling around the Empire. English Heritage specifically notes that he never returned to Britain. ([English Heritage][1])

So for your report, a good way to phrase it would be:

> **Hadrian visited Britain in AD 122 and ordered the construction of the Wall, but he left Britain before the Wall was completed and never returned to see the finished structure.**

One interesting point for a report is that **we don't actually know exactly why Hadrian decided to build the Wall**. A biography written about 200 years after his reign says that he built a wall to separate the Romans from the peoples to the north, but historians have to combine this account with archaeological evidence to understand its purpose. ([English Heritage][1])

That uncertainty could make a good research question: **“Why did Hadrian build his wall?”**

[1]: https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/hadrians-wall/hadrians-wall-history-and-stories/hadrian/?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Emperor Hadrian | English Heritage"

Can you suggest some topic ideas for my paper?

Sure. For a Grade 10 history paper, I'd aim for a topic that is **specific enough to argue**, rather than something broad like “The History of Hadrian's Wall.” Here are some possibilities:

### 🏛️ Politics & Empire

1. **Why did Hadrian build Hadrian's Wall?**
   Examine military defense, controlling movement, displaying Roman power, and managing the northern frontier.

2. **Was Hadrian's Wall primarily a defensive structure or a symbol of Roman power?**
   A good topic because you can compare different interpretations of the evidence.

3. **What does Hadrian's Wall tell us about the limits of the Roman Empire?**
   Explore why Rome stopped expanding northward and how frontiers worked.

### ⚔️ Military History

4. **How effective was Hadrian's Wall as a military frontier?**
   Investigate forts, soldiers, gates, patrols, and the movement of people across the frontier.

5. **Who built and defended Hadrian's Wall?**
   Look at the different Roman military units involved, including soldiers recruited from different parts of the Empire.

6. **What was life like for a Roman soldier stationed on Hadrian's Wall?**
   This would let you use archaeological discoveries and the Vindolanda tablets as primary evidence.

### 👥 People & Everyday Life

7. **Was Hadrian's Wall really a barrier between Romans and Britons?**
   Explore trade, migration, relationships, and evidence of interaction between people on both sides.

8. **What can the Vindolanda tablets tell us about everyday life on Hadrian's Wall?**
   A particularly strong topic if you enjoy working with primary sources.

9. **How did the construction of Hadrian's Wall affect the people living in northern Britain?**
   Consider both Roman communities and local populations.

### 🏗️ Engineering & Construction

10. **How did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall?**
    Investigate materials, construction techniques, organization, and the enormous amount of labor involved.

11. **Why was Hadrian's Wall built where it was?**
    Examine geography, terrain, existing roads and settlements, and the strategic importance of the location.

### 🕰️ Legacy

12. **What happened to Hadrian's Wall after the Romans left Britain?**
    Follow its changing purpose and condition from the 5th century to the present.

13. **How has archaeology changed our understanding of Hadrian's Wall?**
    Compare early interpretations with what excavations and discoveries have revealed.

### ⭐ If you want something especially manageable

I'd shortlist these three:

| Topic                                                               | What makes it interesting                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Why did Hadrian build the Wall?**                                 | Lots of competing interpretations and evidence                      |
| **Was the Wall really a barrier?**                                  | Lets you investigate people, trade, migration, and military control |
| **What can the Vindolanda tablets tell us about life on the Wall?** | Excellent opportunity to use **primary sources**                    |

For a Grade 10 paper, I'd particularly consider **“Was Hadrian's Wall really a barrier?”** because you can build an argument from concrete evidence rather than simply describing the Wall. It also avoids the problem of trying to answer a question historians aren't completely certain about.

### 🏛️ The basics

* **Built:** Around **AD 142**, during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius.
* **Location:** Across central Scotland, roughly from the **Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde**.
* **Length:** About **60 km (37 miles)**.
* **Construction:** Unlike Hadrian's Wall, which was largely stone in its surviving eastern sections, the Antonine Wall was primarily a **turf rampart built on a stone foundation**, with a large defensive ditch on its northern side.
* **Purpose:** It marked the **northern frontier of the Roman Empire in Britain** for a period.
* **Occupation:** The Romans held the Antonine Wall for only about **20 years** before withdrawing south to Hadrian's Wall.

### Hadrian's Wall vs. Antonine Wall

The two walls are particularly interesting to compare:

|                  | **Hadrian's Wall**           | **Antonine Wall**                         |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Built            | c. AD 122                    | c. AD 142                                 |
| Emperor          | Hadrian                      | Antoninus Pius                            |
| Location         | Northern England             | Central Scotland                          |
| Length           | ~117 km / 73 miles           | ~60 km / 37 miles                         |
| Main material    | Mostly stone                 | Turf                                      |
| Roman occupation | Several centuries            | ~20 years                                 |
| Purpose          | Frontier control and defense | Extended the Roman frontier farther north |

One interesting question for your paper would be **“Why did the Romans abandon the Antonine Wall and return to Hadrian's Wall?”** It connects directly to the larger question of how far north the Romans could realistically control Britain.

The Antonine Wall is also part of the **Frontiers of the Roman Empire UNESCO World Heritage Site**, along with Hadrian's Wall and other Roman frontier sites.

What are some of the social and political implications of Hadrian's Wall?

Yes. Hadrian's Wall has **much broader social and political implications** than simply being a military wall. For a Grade 10 paper, these could give you some strong angles for analysis.

### Political implications

**1. It showed the limits of Roman expansion.**
Hadrian's policy was partly about consolidating territory rather than constantly conquering more. The Wall established a defined frontier for Britannia and represented Rome deciding where its political and military control would end. ([English Heritage][1])

**2. It strengthened Roman control over Britain.**
The Wall wasn't simply designed to stop an invading army. Milecastles and gates allowed Roman soldiers to **monitor and control movement**, including travelers and traders. This gave Rome greater administrative control over its northern border. ([English Heritage][1])

**3. It was a statement of Roman power.**
A huge, continuous frontier construction demonstrated the resources and organizational ability of the Roman state. Hadrian's Wall was also famous during its own time, with evidence that people even produced souvenirs depicting the frontier. ([English Heritage][2])

**4. It defined a political boundary between different groups.**
The Wall separated the Roman province of Britannia from territories to the north that Rome did not permanently control. However, the boundary wasn't completely closed: people continued to cross it, trade, and interact.

### Social implications

**5. The Wall created new communities.**
Forts attracted **soldiers, families, traders, craftspeople, and other civilians**. Settlements developed around military installations, meaning the Wall became a place where people actually lived rather than simply a line of defenses. ([English Heritage][3])

**6. It created a remarkably multicultural society.**
People associated with the Wall came from different parts of the Roman Empire. Soldiers included people from areas corresponding to modern **Spain, Romania, Germany, France, the Netherlands, North Africa, and Syria**. Local Britons also lived alongside them. ([English Heritage][4])

This means the Wall can challenge the simplistic idea that **"Romans" and "Britons" were two completely separate groups**. The frontier was actually a place where cultures mixed.

**7. It changed the lives of local populations.**
Roman military occupation brought roads, forts, trade, taxation, and new economic opportunities, but Roman rule also meant that local populations lived under an occupying imperial government. The effects therefore weren't necessarily the same for everyone.

**8. It affected identity.**
Living on a frontier could give people multiple identities: someone might be locally British, serve in a Roman military unit recruited from somewhere else, worship local gods, and participate in Roman society. English Heritage describes the Wall as a place where people from across Europe and North Africa met, traded, served, and adopted aspects of one another's cultures. ([English Heritage][3])

### A potentially strong paper topic

You could turn all of this into a more analytical question:

> **“How did Hadrian's Wall affect the political control and social development of northern Britain?”**

Or, if you want something more interesting and focused:

> **“Did Hadrian's Wall divide people, or bring them together?”**

The second question would allow you to examine the **political purpose of creating a border** while also looking at the surprising evidence that the frontier became a multicultural community. That's a good opportunity for a Grade 10 paper because you aren't just explaining what the Wall was—you'd be **using evidence to examine two different effects of the same historical event**.
